outcome: Neither part of the problem is settled or claimed settled as of 11 Oct 2026: the infinitude of regular primes and the e^(−1/2) relative density remain open. The one in-window preprint bearing on regular primes (Axiom Math, arXiv:2602.05090, 4 Feb 2026, AxiomProver-generated Lean proof) proves a density-one statement about truncated regularity (M_α(p)-regularity, indices up to about √p/(log p)^α), which produces no regular prime and bounds neither the infinitude nor the density of regular primes.
problem_asks: (1) Whether there are infinitely many regular primes. A regular prime is an odd prime p that does not divide the class number of Q(ζ_p); by Kummer's criterion, p divides none of the numerators of B₂, B₄, …, B_(p−3). (2) If (1) holds, whether the relative density of the regular primes among all primes is e^(−1/2) ≈ 0.6065, i.e. whether the proportion of primes ≤ n that are regular tends to e^(−1/2). Part (2) is conditional on part (1) in the wording given.

events.what_happened: Hart, Harvey and Ong computed all irregular primes below 2^31 = 2,147,483,648, verified the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture for each, and checked the index-of-irregularity structure of the p-part of the class group of Q(ζ_p). Posted to arXiv as 1605.02398; published Math. Comp. 86 (2017) per a search snippet. Pre-window computation; the Wikipedia article cites it for the observed proportion of regular primes below 2^31 (60.6590%) that supports the e^(−1/2) heuristic. The abstract itself does not mention density.
events.revisions: v1 only (9 May 2016). Journal version: Math. Comp. 86 (2017), 3031–3049 (per search snippet; journal page not opened).
events.delivers: A finite computation: every irregular prime below 2^31, with Kummer–Vandiver verified for each. It establishes finitely many instances of statements about irregular primes and says nothing about whether regular primes are infinite. Its bearing on the density question is empirical only: the Wikipedia article uses it as support for the e^(−1/2) prediction; the abstract makes no density claim.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the infinitude of regular primes and the relative density e^(−1/2).

events.direction: Neutral toward the problem. It supports the empirical picture (irregular primes of each index occur in the Poisson-type proportions predicted by the heuristic) and says nothing either way about infinitude.

The Chinese abstract (as seen in a snippet) lists the chain starting at A_2 and omits A_0. The journal page fetch failed (certificate expired), so this is from snippets only.

events.what_happened: Axiom Math posted arXiv:2602.05090, 'Almost all primes are partially regular' (submitted 4 Feb 2026, 22:20:52 UTC; 21 authors including Evan Chen, Kenny Lau, Ken Ono, Seewoo Lee and Jujian Zhang). The main theorem (Theorem 1.1 in the arXiv version) states that for fixed α > 1/2, the number of primes p ≤ X that are not M_α(p)-regular is O_α(X/(log X)^(2α)), where M_α(p) = ⌊√p/(log p)^α⌋. An odd prime is m-regular when p divides no numerator of B₂ₖ for even 2 ≤ 2k ≤ min(m, p−3). So almost all primes are M_α(p)-regular. Via Leopoldt reflection the paper derives a partial Vandiver statement for the even eigenspaces A_p(ω^(2k)) in the same index range. The arXiv v1 is the only version found. Axiom's blog post (5 Feb 2026, by CEO Carina Hong) describes the main engine as 'autonomously proved and formalized in Lean by AxiomProver, starting from a natural-language statement'. The blog calls the density result Theorem 1.3, while the arXiv version numbers it Theorem 1.1.
events.revisions: v1 only (4 Feb 2026) as of 11 Oct 2026. No v2 found in search or on the arXiv abstract page as fetched.
events.delivers: For each fixed α > 1/2, a density-one set of primes p satisfies: p divides no numerator of B₂ₖ for even 2 ≤ 2k ≤ min(M_α(p), p−3), where M_α(p) ≈ √p/(log p)^α. The bound is O-type with a constant depending on α (a later AxiomProver run in the repository finds that C_α = 10 works, per Remark 1.2 and the repo's extension/ folder). Restrictions: this is M-regularity, a condition implied by regularity but much weaker, because it only checks indices up to about √p/(log p)^α rather than up to p−3. Since M_α(p) is asymptotically smaller than p−3, the theorem does not show that any particular prime is regular, and it gives no lower bound on the proportion of regular primes.
events.remains: The infinitude of regular primes (nothing here produces a regular prime). The relative density e^(−1/2) (full regularity, which needs every index up to p−3, is not reached). The full range of indices is outside the reach of the density statement.

events.directly_checkable: The natural-language claim is in problem.tex (#{p ≤ X prime : p not M_α(p)-regular} = O(X/(log X)^(2α))); the formal version is the Lean declaration irregular_primes_asymptotic in PartialRegularity/solution.lean. Whether the Lean statement matches problem.tex, and whether the regularity definitions are right, can be checked by reading. I did not do it.
events.doubts: (a) The formal translation of the problem statement (PartialRegularity/problem.lean) is itself listed in the repo as produced by the system, so the faithfulness of the formal statement to the natural-language claim rests on reading; I found no report of an outside party doing that reading. (b) The paper is a single version with no peer review found. (c) Remark 1.9 calls AxiomProver 'an AI tool currently under development' and does not give a version. (d) The company's blog calls the result a 'Partial Vandiver Conjecture', while the paper calls it partial regularity and a partial Vandiver theorem; the framing differs. (e) Theorem numbering (1.1 in arXiv, 1.3 in the blog) and Lean version (4.34.0-rc2 vs 4.26.0) are inconsistent across sources. (f) The Lean declaration is named irregular_primes_asymptotic although it bounds the count of non-M-regular primes, which may mislead a reader. None of these is a demonstrated error; they are the points a reviewer would check.
events.direction: Does not bear on whether regular primes are infinite or on their density. It proves a statement about truncated regularity holding for almost all primes. That statement is consistent with any density of regular primes, because regular primes are a subset of M_α(p)-regular primes. It is therefore silent on the problem's question, not supportive or opposed to a particular answer.

systems.name: AxiomProver
systems.what_it_did: Given the natural-language statement of the density claim (the arXiv's Theorem 1.1) together with a self-contained list of definitions, it generated a Lean/Mathlib statement and a complete verified proof with no hints, per Section 4 and Remark 1.9. The paper describes it as 'an AI tool currently under development' (so a pre-release or internal tool, not a shipped model). The repo's README says the system also produced the formal translation of the problem statement (problem.lean) and the formal solution (solution.lean). In an internal experiment it found that C_α = 10 works for all α > 1/2. The authors say it was not asked to re-prove the deep external theorems of Ribet or Leopoldt. This is load-bearing for the result: the proof of the density theorem is the system's.
systems.basis_quote: given only the natural-language statement of the claim. No human assistance was provided.

events.what_happened: Xuejun Guo and Zhengyu Tao, 'Density of Vanishing of Certain Eigenspaces of Cyclotomic Class Groups' (arXiv:2609.13932, 12 Sep 2026). For even d ≥ 4 with N = (p−1)/d and primes p ≡ d+1 (mod 2d), it bounds the odd block ⊕A_{aN} and, by reflection, the even block ⊕A_{p−aN}. For d ∈ {4, 6} both blocks vanish on a relative density-one set of primes. A_34 = 0 is stated for every odd prime p. The reference list cites Chen et al. (arXiv:2602.05090) as [5] (HTML version read).
events.delivers: Density-one vanishing of certain eigenspace blocks of the class group of Q(ζ_p), restricted to primes in residue classes p ≡ d+1 (mod 2d) with d ∈ {4, 6} (for the full vanishing), and an index-specific statement A_34 = 0 for every odd prime. It is a Vandiver-type statement. It does not mention regular primes, their infinitude, or their density.
events.doubts: The body of the PDF could not be read through the fetch tool (binary), so the statements are taken from the abstract page and the HTML reference list. The A_34 claim is a single-index statement that I did not check against the body.
events.direction: Neutral toward the problem. It is a neighbouring Vandiver-type density result and does not mention regular primes.

events.what_happened: On 4 Sep 2026 Anthropic published a research post and GitHub repository (anthropics/fermats-last-theorem, Apache-2.0) stating that Claude produced a machine-checked Lean 4 / Mathlib formalisation of the full Fermat's Last Theorem for exponents n ≥ 3. The post says 'Claude worked largely autonomously over 11 days', 'Dozens of Claude agents collaborated to define concepts, prove intermediate theorems', and that the proof 'follows a simplified version of Wiles's proof from Darmon, Diamond, and Taylor'. It reports about 13 million lines of Lean, 30,300 intermediate theorems proved (29,500 used in the final proof), and about six billion output tokens. Coordination used Prove2Me. The post says human input was 'limited to occasional high-level instructions from Tianyi', that 'what's novel here is the verification', and it thanks Kevin Buzzard for reviewing the proof. This is a formalisation of a theorem proved in 1995, not of Kummer's argument, and the post does not mention regular primes, Kummer or Vandiver.
events.revisions: Repository lists 3 commits; no dated revisions found. Secondary coverage gives 5 Sep for the announcement; the post itself is dated Sep 4, 2026.
events.delivers: A machine-checked proof of FLT for exponents n ≥ 3 (positive a, b, c), per the README's main theorem fermat_last_theorem. It verifies Wiles's theorem by the modularity route, not Kummer's regular-prime method. It says nothing about which primes are regular.

summary: Nothing settles, or is claimed to settle, either part of the problem since 26 January 2024: no proof that regular primes are infinite, and no proof or disproof of relative density e^(−1/2). The searches covered the problem's name and variants, the density conjecture, Kummer/Vandiver/Bernoulli wording, the in-window results, and AI involvement. The one in-window item that bears on regular primes is arXiv:2602.05090 (Axiom Math, posted 4 Feb 2026). Its main theorem is that for fixed α > 1/2 almost all primes are M_α(p)-regular, where M_α(p) = ⌊√p/(log p)^α⌋. I read the arXiv HTML (statement, Remark 1.9, Sections 4.1 and 4.2 via a summarising fetch), Axiom's blog post, the GitHub README, and the Lean solution and problem files (the Lean file was read in two halves through a summarising fetch; no sorry or axiom was reported; I did not compile it). The theorem concerns truncated regularity. A prime is regular only if p divides no numerator B₂ₖ for all even 2k up to p−3, while M_α(p) is asymptotically smaller than p−3. So the theorem produces no regular prime and gives neither a lower bound on the proportion of regular primes nor evidence for the infinitude question. The authors call it partial regularity and a partial Vandiver theorem; the company's blog calls it a 'Partial Vandiver Conjecture'. On AI involvement, the authors' own text is clear: Section 4.1 says the claim was 'given only the natural-language statement of the claim. No human assistance was provided.' Section 4.2 says 'the human authors wrote this paper (without the use of AI) for human readers.' Remark 1.9 calls AxiomProver 'an AI tool currently under development' and says it 'generated a Lean/Mathlib statement and a fully verified proof.' The repo README also says the system produced the formal translation of the problem statement (problem.lean), so the faithfulness of that translation to problem.tex rests on reading, and I found no report of an outside party doing it. Human engagement with the preprint is limited to an acknowledgement that Ken Ribet, Ashvin Swaminathan and Ila Varma commented on an earlier version; the content of their comments is not stated. Ken Ono and Kenny Lau are among the authors, so they are not outside checks. The search results also contain AI-generated literature summaries (themoonlight.io); I did not use them as evidence. The only later paper I found that cites the result is arXiv:2609.13932 (Guo and Tao, 12 Sep 2026), which cites it as [5] for a density-one vanishing statement and does not mention regular primes. The second in-window AI-involved item is Anthropic's Lean formalisation of the full Fermat's Last Theorem (4 Sep 2026). It formalises Wiles's proof of a known theorem, not Kummer's regular-prime argument, and its post does not mention regular primes, Kummer or Vandiver. Under §5.4 I have not put it in ai.systems, because it formalises an argument already proven by humans, but the AI involvement is large (dozens of Claude agents, about six billion output tokens, and 'Claude worked largely autonomously'). The regular-prime Lean formalisation (Best et al., arXiv:2410.01466, Oct 2024) and the 2023 first-case formalisation are human-written per their abstracts, and neither touches infinitude or density. Pre-window items: Hart, Harvey and Ong's computation of irregular primes below 2^31 (2016), which Wikipedia cites as empirical support for the density heuristic but whose abstract does not mention density; Seki's 2023 preprint restating infinitude as open; and Qin's 2024 Acta Math. Sinica paper, read only through search snippets because the journal page's certificate had expired; its English and Chinese abstracts disagree on whether A_0 is in the vanishing chain. Close call on the Axiom event: the e^(−1/2) heuristic is itself a statement about Bernoulli numerators avoiding p, so a density-one theorem about those divisibilities is in the same mechanism, and on that reading the event moves a quantity the problem names, though only in truncated form. The stricter reading is that the counted quantity is M-regularity, not regularity, so the problem's own density is not moved. Both readings are recorded for the judging pass. Searches for AI involvement specific to this problem (GPT, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, Claude with Kummer or Bernoulli wording, and ML on irregular primes) found no claims beyond those above.
competing_reading: The Axiom result could be counted as moving the problem's own quantity. The e^(−1/2) heuristic (Siegel) rests on the Bernoulli numerators behaving independently modulo p, so a density-one theorem about which primes avoid Bernoulli-numerator divisibility is a step in the same direction, and the authors' result is the first of its type. On that reading the event moves a quantity the problem names, but only over a truncated index range. The stricter reading is that the quantity moved is M-regularity, a weaker property implied by regularity, and that M-regularity does not move the density of regular primes or the infinitude question. A second reading of the Axiom paper's AI role is that 'No human assistance was provided' refers only to the proof run, not to the choice of statement, definitions, and formal translation, all of which the repo says were produced or fed by humans in the setup.
what_would_settle_it: For the density question: a proof that the proportion of primes p with no p dividing any numerator of B₂ₖ for 2 ≤ 2k ≤ p−3 converges to e^(−1/2), or to any positive limit. For infinitude: a proof that infinitely many such primes exist, or that the set is finite. For the Axiom event specifically: an independent human check of the Lean formal statement against problem.tex and of the paper's use of the Herbrand–Ribet and Leopoldt results; a published referee report; and a reconciliation of the Lean version and Theorem numbering across the repo, the paper and the blog. For the AI question: the full PDF's acknowledgements and contribution statement, to confirm that nothing beyond Remark 1.9 and Section 4 describes the system's role.
